5.2 Option Basics

Calls and puts

Section titled “Calls and puts”

A forward contract (5.1 Forwards and Futures) is an obligation: at maturity the trade must happen at the agreed price. An option is a right: its buyer can choose whether to use it.

  • A call option gives its buyer the right to buy the underlying asset at an agreed price KKK on (or before) the expiry date.
  • A put option gives its buyer the right to sell the underlying asset at the price KKK.

KKK is called the strike price. An option that can be exercised only on the expiry date is European; one that can be exercised at any time before expiry is American. The price the buyer pays the seller (also called the writer) for this right is the option premium.

At expiry the buyer exercises only when it pays, so the payoff is never negative:

CT=max⁡(ST−K, 0)PT=max⁡(K−ST, 0)C_T = \max(S_T - K,\ 0) \qquad P_T = \max(K - S_T,\ 0)CT​=max(ST​−K, 0)PT​=max(K−ST​, 0)

CTC_TCT​ is the payoff of a call at expiry and PTP_TPT​ that of a put. The buyer’s profit is the payoff minus the premium; the writer’s profit is the opposite. When the stock price is above the strike, a call is in the money; below it, out of the money; equal to it, at the money; for a put it is the other way round.

Check C1
An investor sells (writes) a call option without owning the stock, collecting the premium. His largest possible loss is:
Whose largest loss is the premium? At expiry he must pay max⁡(ST−K,0)\max(S_T - K, 0)max(ST​−K,0). Does that grow as the price rises?
A call writer loses when the price rises. Is there a limit to how far the price can rise?
That is the case of a put writer if the price falls to 0. When does a call writer lose?

Intrinsic value and time value

Section titled “Intrinsic value and time value”

Before expiry, an option’s price can be split into two parts: the intrinsic value, what immediate exercise would bring, max⁡(S−K, 0)\max(S - K,\ 0)max(S−K, 0) for a call; and the part above the intrinsic value, called the time value.

Time value comes from the asymmetry of the payoff: the stock price will keep moving before expiry; when it moves favorably the option’s payoff rises with it, and when it moves unfavorably the loss is at most the premium. The more the price swings and the longer until expiry, the more this asymmetry is worth. 5.3 Option Pricing turns this idea into a pricing formula.

Check C2
An at-the-money call with 6 months to expiry has an intrinsic value of 0, so its price should be close to 0.
Think: the price will keep moving over 6 months. How does the option's payoff change if the price rises? What is the most its holder can lose if the price falls?

Common strategies

Section titled “Common strategies”

Combining options with the stock changes the shape of the payoff:

  • A protective put: hold the stock and buy a put. When the stock falls below the strike, the put’s payoff offsets the stock’s loss, so the worst outcome is capped, like buying insurance on the stock (1.4 Choice Under Uncertainty).
  • A covered call: hold the stock and sell a call, collecting the premium. When the stock rises above the strike, the stock’s gain is offset by the loss on the call.

Combining the two (buying a put and selling a call) is called a collar, often used to limit the range of gains and losses over a period without selling the stock.

An executive holds a large amount of his company's stock and cannot sell it for a year. He worries about a big fall but does not want to spend much cash on protection. Which approach fits his needs best?

What do calls do when the price falls?

Employee stock options

Section titled “Employee stock options”

Many companies, especially technology companies and startups, pay part of their employees’ compensation in stock options. An employee stock option is essentially a long-dated call struck at the share price on the grant date, but it differs from exchange-traded options in several ways:

  • The term is long, usually 10 years.
  • It must vest, for example in installments over 4 years; unvested options are usually forfeited when the employee leaves, and vested ones often must be exercised within a short time.
  • It cannot be sold, and company policy usually also forbids employees to hedge it with other derivatives.
  • The tax treatment of exercising and selling is complicated (6.5 Accounts and Taxes (US)).

For the employee, this means that wealth and job income are concentrated in the same company (4.12 Life-Cycle Asset Allocation Theory). For the company’s existing shareholders, the options cost no cash, but they dilute their ownership when exercised.

Check C5
An employee receives 10-year options from his company, still vesting, which cannot be sold or hedged. Compared with options of the same terms traded on an exchange, these options are worth to him:
The long term is already in the exchange-traded option "of the same terms". What really differs between them?
Can he sell them or hedge the risk when needed, as a holder of exchange-traded options can?
Even if he knows the company well, can he diversify this risk? How is it related to his job income?

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • A call is the right to buy at KKK, with payoff max⁡(ST−K,0)\max(S_T - K, 0)max(ST​−K,0) at expiry; a put is the right to sell at KKK, with payoff max⁡(K−ST,0)\max(K - S_T, 0)max(K−ST​,0); the buyer pays a premium.
  • Option price = intrinsic value + time value; time value comes from the asymmetry of the payoff and is higher with more volatility and a longer term.
  • A protective put caps the worst outcome at the cost of the premium; a covered call collects a premium at the cost of giving up gains above the strike.
  • Employee stock options are long-dated, must vest, and cannot be sold or hedged, so the employee’s wealth and job income are concentrated in the same company.

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1
A stock is at 100 dollars. A 3-month call with a strike of 100 costs 6 dollars. An investor has 6,000 dollars and thinks the stock will rise.
(a) At expiry, what is the lowest stock price at which buying the call does not lose money? If the stock is at 90, 110 or 130 dollars in 3 months, what are the returns from putting all 6,000 dollars into the stock and from putting it all into calls?
(b) He says: "With calls the most I can lose is the premium, so they are less risky than the stock." Evaluate this statement.
Question 2
A retiree puts all 1 million dollars into a stock index and, at the start of each year, buys 1-year puts with a strike at 90% of the index level then, paying a premium of 2.53% of the index. By his estimate, the chance that the index ends below the strike is about 20%, in which case the puts pay on average 6% of the index.
(a) What is his worst loss in any year, in percent (ignoring dividends and interest on the premium)? By his estimate, by how many percentage points does the insurance reduce his return on average each year?
(b) He says: "I buy insurance every year, so holding 100% stocks carries no risk, and my returns are unaffected." Evaluate this statement. What else could lower his worst loss?
Question 3
A "high-income" fund advertises: "We hold stocks and each month sell 1-month calls with a strike 5% above the share price, collecting about 0.73% a month in premiums. With dividends, we pay investors a very high distribution yield."
(a) At 0.73% a month, about how much do the premiums come to over a year (without compounding)? If in some month the stock goes from 100 to 115, or from 100 to 90, what is the fund's return that month (per 100 dollars of stock, ignoring dividends)?
(b) Evaluate calling the premiums a "distribution yield". In what kind of market does such a fund clearly lag the stocks it holds?
Question 4
At a startup, the CFO tells a candidate: "We're giving you 10,000 options, worth 15 dollars each by an option pricing model, so that's 150,000 dollars of pay. And the company doesn't pay a cent in cash, so they cost the company almost nothing." The options vest over 4 years, expire in 10, cannot be sold, and employees are not allowed to hedge them.
Evaluate both statements. In comparing this job with another that pays 30,000 dollars more in cash and has no options, what should the candidate consider?
